My responsibilities are to my god, myself, my family (marriage, then my children, then my parents and siblings), my relatives, my community, my city/town, my state/province, my region, and then my country in that very order. I do not engage myself with any of my families concerns until mine are addressed first. I do not engage myself with my relatives concerns until my families are addressed first. I do not engage myself with my communities concerns until my relatives are addressed first and I'm sure you can get the gist of how I prioritize.

The question you're asking isn't, "Would you help your hungry neighbor," but rather, "should you feed your hungry neighbor." To answer that question, no you should not. If you didn't help your neighbor learn to feed himself before their pantry was empty, you gain nothing by encouraging them to become dependent upon you to you feed them later. When neighbors ask if they might come over to see how you've stocked and they aren't prepping themselves, make the counter offer to come over and help them start a small garden. I keep a variety of spare inexpensive gardening tools and burpee seeds precisely for this purpose.

The reasoning in this approach is simple. As the decline becomes more and more apparent, there will be a steady shift in psychology. As this shift progresses, you do not want to find yourself or your family suddenly surrounded by potential enemies or highly aggressive competitors who've out grouped you, especially if you currently have young children and/or a wife who in anyway expresses feminist thinking. Always make the offer to share your knowledge, not your resources.

Remember, we're talking about adapting to an otherwise unexpected collapse of the economy, utilities, and/or food distribution which cripples or completely takes down the various fences of security our civilization depends on. "Autonomy" from natures perspective may not be in sync with "autonomy" from the perspective of the civilized mind. My prioritizing my needs ahead of others isn't an inflexible mindset. I can say that I would reduce my calorie intake to provide a proper nutrition load for a child as there are long term consequences to a child's health when you deprive them. However, you will not be immune from this yourself. If that child's survival is utterly dependent upon your own, an inflexible sacrificing mindset could ultimately be detrimental to your mutual survival, rather than a benefit.

This is why I always advise preppers to share their knowledge with others in their community, not their own resources. Helping your neighbor build a small garden with cheap corporate seed stock provides them with basic skills they can expand on to keep their family fed. Helping your neighbors to learn how to reduce their homes dependence upon the power grid, reduces their monthly expenses, and ensures their home is self sufficient in a power outage. Helping your neighbors to secure their own International Amateur Radio Union member radio operators license, means when the communications networks go down, they aren't in the dark. Inviting your neighbor to jog with you in the morning, helps them to loose those excess pounds they've been meaning to shed.

In order to be an effective prepper, you must aspire to be a successful prepper.
